tier_reason: Upgraded from C to B. The code is public after all: ix-project/ix (MIT text), plus ix-project/ix-bench, whose README says it holds the scripts that run the benchmarks and plot the graphs of the OSDI 2014 paper (bench_memcached.py). The paper is peer-reviewed, compares against Linux 3.16.1 with libevent+epoll and stock memcached-1.4.18, and names the server CPU (Xeon E5-2665 @ 2.4 GHz). It is not A because neither the paper nor the release states a compiler version. Flags appear only in build files (dp/Makefile gcc -O3; ix-bench Makefile gcc -O2), none for memcached, and the release dates from 2016, two years after the paper.

corrections.baseline: Linux 3.16.1 kernel TCP stack via libevent + epoll: stock memcached-1.4.18 on tuned Linux (pinned threads, IRQ affinity, tuned interrupt moderation); mTCP is a second baseline in the microbenchmarks
corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: IX 'improves the throughput of a widely deployed, key-value store by up to 3.6x and reduces tail latency by more than 2x'. Sec 5.5 / Table 2 (memcached vs Linux): 2.8x (ETC, 550K -> 1550K RPS) and 3.6x (USR, 500K -> 1800K RPS) at a 500us 99th-percentile SLA. Unloaded 99th-percentile latency is 94 -> 45us (ETC) and 85 -> 32us (USR). Microbenchmarks: up to 10x the throughput of Linux and 1.9x of mTCP for short messages on 10GbE; one-way 64B latency 5.7us vs 24us for Linux (4x).
corrections.workload: memcached-1.4.18 ported to IX's libix event API vs stock memcached on Linux. The mutilate load generator ran Facebook ETC (20-70B keys, 1B-1KB values, 75% GET) and USR (<20B keys, 2B values, 99% GET) workloads from 23 Linux client machines over 1,476 TCP connections. Metrics are max RPS at a 500us 99th-percentile SLA and unloaded 99th-percentile latency. The paper also has NetPIPE ping-pong, short-message echo and connection-scaling (up to 250K connections) microbenchmarks.
corrections.hardware: Server: Intel Xeon E5-2665 @ 2.4 GHz (8 cores / 16 hyperthreads per socket), 256 GB DRAM, Intel x520 10GbE NICs (82599EB), either 1 port or 4x10GbE bonded. Clients: Xeon E5-2637 @ 3.5 GHz and E5-2650 @ 2.6 GHz running Linux. Switch: Quanta/Cumulus 48x10GbE (Broadcom Trident+). OS: Ubuntu 14.04 with the Linux 3.16.1 kernel. For memcached, Linux used 8 cores and IX used 6.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The 2016 code release's build files show dp/Makefile building the IX dataplane with gcc -O3 -mno-red-zone -fno-pie, and ix-bench/Makefile building its libevent/epoll client/server with gcc -O2. No compiler version is given anywhere, and no memcached build flags are given.
corrections.caveats: OSDI 2014 peer-reviewed paper. The code was released in May 2016 (ix-project/ix and ix-project/ix-bench, whose scripts cover the OSDI'14 and SoCC'15 graphs), so the released code may differ from the 2014 prototype. The paper says outright that its Linux benchmarks use 'the libevent framework with the epoll system call' and that memcached is built on libevent. The win is over the Linux kernel TCP stack plus epoll, not over the event loop alone. IX's best config used 6 cores against Linux's 8. memcached was ported to IX's libix API, and the clients ran Linux. Running IX needs VT-x (Dune), DPDK, supported Intel NICs (the README lists 82599/X520/X540) and dedicated polling hardware threads and NIC queues. License: IX's own code is the MIT text under an 'IX Open Source License' header, so GitHub reports NOASSERTION. It statically links libdune from the ix-project/dune submodule, which has no license file, and needs GPL kernel modules (dune.ko MODULE_LICENSE GPL; pcidma GPL-2.0) plus DPDK. The paper says the dataplane is 41% derived from the DPDK ixgbe driver, 26% from lwIP and 15% from Dune. There have been no commits since 2017-11-06.

notes: The record's 'no public code' premise is wrong. The orchestrator should set repo_url to https://github.com/ix-project/ix (C, not archived, not a fork, 136 stars), which is outside the allowed correction fields. The paper numbers (3.6x, 2.8x, >2x tail, 10x/1.9x) were checked in the abstract, Sec 1, Sec 5.5 and Table 2. The license was read from the LICENSE text, and the libdune licensing gap is why usability is 'mixed'.
